### Problem: Ball in Berland {#sec-cnt-pcomp-ball}

::: {.p-statement}
A class has $a$ boys and $b$ girls, and $k$ **distinct** boy–girl couples $(a_i, b_i)$ are willing to dance together. Choose **two** of the $k$ couples so that no person is in both — the two couples share neither a boy nor a girl. Count the ways (unordered). There are $t$ test cases.

Sample: $a = 3$, $b = 4$, $k = 4$ with couples $(1,2), (1,3), (2,2), (3,4)$ gives $4$. A single couple ($k = 1$) gives $0$. With $a = b = 2$ and all four couples $(1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (2,2)$ the answer is $2$.

Constraints: $1 \le t \le 10^4$, $1 \le a, b, k \le 2 \cdot 10^5$, and the sums of $a$, $b$ and $k$ over the test cases are at most $2 \cdot 10^5$ each.

Source: [CF 1475C · Ball in Berland](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1475/C){.solved rating="1400"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Counting good pairs of couples directly means checking two conditions; counting the **bad** ones means counting pairs that share a boy, plus pairs that share a girl. Two couples share boy $x$ in $\binom{\deg x}{2}$ ways, so the pairs sharing *some* boy number $\sum_x \binom{\deg_A x}{2}$, and likewise for girls. The two bad events could overlap only for two couples sharing both people — the same couple twice, which distinctness forbids. Inclusion–exclusion therefore has nothing to add back:
$$\text{answer} = \binom{k}{2} - \sum_{\text{boys } x} \binom{\deg_A x}{2} - \sum_{\text{girls } y} \binom{\deg_B y}{2}.$$
On the sample, boy $1$ and girl $2$ each have degree $2$, so the answer is $\binom{4}{2} - 1 - 1 = 4$.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Test every pair of couples.** $O(k^2)$ — about $2 \cdot 10^{10}$ pairs at the limit.
2. **Complement per couple.** Couple $(x, y)$ conflicts with the other $\deg_A x - 1$ couples of boy $x$ and the other $\deg_B y - 1$ couples of girl $y$ (never the same couple twice), so it is compatible with $(k - 1) - (\deg_A x - 1) - (\deg_B y - 1)$ couples. Sum over couples and halve, because each good pair is seen from both ends. $O(k + a + b)$.
3. **Complement globally (inclusion–exclusion).** $\binom{k}{2}$ minus the same-boy pairs minus the same-girl pairs, plus the both-shared pairs, which are $0$. $O(k + a + b)$, and the form that names the principle.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Test every pair of couples

::: {.form-next}
The statement: two couples are good when their boys differ and their girls differ. Quadratic in $k$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def ball_brute(boys, girls):
    k, ans = len(boys), 0
    for p in range(k):
        for q in range(p + 1, k):
            if boys[p] != boys[q] and girls[p] != girls[q]:
                ans += 1
    return ans


assert ball_brute([1, 1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 2, 4]) == 4
assert ball_brute([1], [1]) == 0
assert ball_brute([1, 1, 2, 2], [1, 2, 1, 2]) == 2
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
int main() {
    int t;
    scanf("%d", &t);
    while (t--) {
        int a, b, k;
        scanf("%d %d %d", &a, &b, &k);
        vector<int> x(k), y(k);
        for (auto& v : x) scanf("%d", &v);
        for (auto& v : y) scanf("%d", &v);
        long long ans = 0;
        for (int p = 0; p < k; ++p)
            for (int q = p + 1; q < k; ++q)
                if (x[p] != x[q] && y[p] != y[q]) ++ans;
        printf("%lld\n", ans);
    }
}
```
:::

#### Complement per couple

::: {.form-next}
Fix one couple and count its bad partners by degree: the other couples of the same boy, plus the other couples of the same girl. Everything else is a good partner. Each good pair is counted from both of its couples, so halve the sum.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def ball_per_couple(boys, girls):
    k = len(boys)
    db, dg = Counter(boys), Counter(girls)
    seen_twice = sum((k - 1) - (db[x] - 1) - (dg[y] - 1) for x, y in zip(boys, girls))
    return seen_twice // 2


assert ball_per_couple([1, 1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 2, 4]) == 4
assert ball_per_couple([1, 1, 2, 2], [1, 2, 1, 2]) == 2
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
int main() {
    int t;
    scanf("%d", &t);
    while (t--) {
        int a, b, k;
        scanf("%d %d %d", &a, &b, &k);
        vector<int> x(k), y(k);
        vector<long long> db(a + 1, 0), dg(b + 1, 0);
        for (auto& v : x) { scanf("%d", &v); ++db[v]; }
        for (auto& v : y) { scanf("%d", &v); ++dg[v]; }
        long long twice = 0;
        for (int p = 0; p < k; ++p) twice += (k - 1) - (db[x[p]] - 1) - (dg[y[p]] - 1);
        printf("%lld\n", twice / 2);
    }
}
```
:::

#### Complement globally (inclusion–exclusion)

::: {.form-next}
Sum the per-couple form over all couples and it collapses: $\binom{k}{2}$ minus $\binom{\deg}{2}$ for every boy and every girl. The term that inclusion–exclusion would add back — pairs sharing a boy *and* a girl — is $0$ because the couples are distinct.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def ball_incl_excl(boys, girls):
    k = len(boys)
    same_boy = sum(math.comb(c, 2) for c in Counter(boys).values())
    same_girl = sum(math.comb(c, 2) for c in Counter(girls).values())
    both = 0                                   # a repeated couple; distinctness rules it out
    return math.comb(k, 2) - same_boy - same_girl + both


assert ball_incl_excl([1, 1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 2, 4]) == 4
assert ball_incl_excl([1], [1]) == 0
assert ball_incl_excl([1, 1, 2, 2], [1, 2, 1, 2]) == 2
for _ in range(300):
    pairs = random.sample([(x, y) for x in range(1, 5) for y in range(1, 5)], random.randint(1, 12))
    bs, gs = [p[0] for p in pairs], [p[1] for p in pairs]
    assert ball_incl_excl(bs, gs) == ball_per_couple(bs, gs) == ball_brute(bs, gs)
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
int main() {
    int t;
    scanf("%d", &t);
    while (t--) {
        int a, b, k;
        scanf("%d %d %d", &a, &b, &k);
        vector<long long> db(a + 1, 0), dg(b + 1, 0);
        for (int p = 0; p < k; ++p) { int v; scanf("%d", &v); ++db[v]; }
        for (int p = 0; p < k; ++p) { int v; scanf("%d", &v); ++dg[v]; }
        long long ans = 1LL * k * (k - 1) / 2;
        for (long long c : db) ans -= c * (c - 1) / 2;   // pairs sharing a boy
        for (long long c : dg) ans -= c * (c - 1) / 2;   // pairs sharing a girl
        printf("%lld\n", ans);                           // + pairs sharing both = 0
    }
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Test every pair of couples**: $O(k^2)$ time, $O(k)$ space. **Complement per couple**: $O(k + a + b)$ time and space. **Complement globally (inclusion–exclusion)**: $O(k + a + b)$ time and space. The answer reaches $\binom{2 \cdot 10^5}{2} \approx 2 \cdot 10^{10}$, so it needs 64 bits; the degree tables must be re-allocated (or cleared over $1..a$ and $1..b$ only) per test, never over the full $2 \cdot 10^5$ range each time.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $k = 1$: $\binom{1}{2} = 0$, nothing to choose.
- Every couple shares one boy: all $\binom{k}{2}$ pairs are bad, answer $0$.
- A complete bipartite set of couples ($a \cdot b = k$): the answer is $\binom{k}{2} - a\binom{b}{2} - b\binom{a}{2}$, which is $2$ for $a = b = 2$, the third sample.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Subtracting the both-shared pairs again.** With distinct couples there are none; if the input could repeat a couple, inclusion–exclusion would add those pairs *back*, not subtract them.
- **Forgetting to halve the per-couple sum.** Each good pair is counted from both couples; the unhalved sample gives $8$.
- **Clearing tables of size $2 \cdot 10^5$ per test.** With $t = 10^4$ tests that is $2 \cdot 10^9$ writes; size the tables by $a$ and $b$.
:::

**Variants.** @sec-cnt-pcomp-unequal has disjoint bad events, so plain subtraction is enough; here the bad events are "same boy" and "same girl", whose overlap had to be checked (and turned out empty). Inclusion–exclusion over more events is in the further reading.
